study_identification_part.si3_author_journal_year: Xiao et al., Biological Psychiatry Global Open Science, 2024
study_identification_part.si4_title: Deviations From Normative Functioning Underlying Emotional Episodic Memory Revealed Cross-Scale Neurodiverse Alterations Linked to Affective Symptoms in Distinct Psychiatric Disorders

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To investigate cross-scale neural dysfunctions related to affective symptoms in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD), bipolar disorder (BD), and schizophrenia (SZ) using normative modeling of functional activation during emotional episodic memory task, and to identify cellular abnormalities underlying macroscale alterations.

SPM12 was used with standardized protocol including slice-timing correction, realignment, segmentation, normalization to MNI, and spatial smoothing. The Desikan-Killiany atlas was used for brain parcellation.
rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.supporting_text: The high-resolution structural T1-weighted MRI and fMRI blood oxygen level-dependent signal were acquired and preprocessed using SPM12 (http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm) with a standardized protocol. The preprocessing of functional imaging was preprocessed using the SPM12 with a standardized protocol whose details can be found elsewhere. Specifically, image processing included 1) excluding the first 4 images as dummy scans; 2) performing slice-timing correction in remaining images; 3) realigning remaining images to the first volume for head motion correction using a six-parameter (rigid body) linear transformation; 4) conducting brain tissue segmentation and spatial normalization using the standard stereotaxic space of Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) template; 5) performing the spatial smoothing with a Gaussian filter set at 8mm full-width at half-maximum.
rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.location: Main text, Image Acquisition and Preprocessing section; Supplementary Page 6-7

nm8_nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study addresses some aspects of nuisance structure: (1) Movement parameters were modeled as nuisance covariates in preprocessing; (2) Age and sex effects were evaluated in sensitivity analysis (Figure S5) showing no significant effect on the normative model; (3) Medication effects were evaluated and found to have no significant correlation with regional deviations. However, site/scanner differences between HCtrain and clinical datasets were not explicitly handled through harmonization or modeling. The study relied on the same scanner model (3T GE Discovery MR750) at both sites but did not explicitly account for potential site effects in the normative model.
nm8_nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: Incorrect responses and residual movement parameters were also modeled as regressors of no interest. Age and age are widely used clinically covariables to construct normative models, to further depict the age trend under different sex conditions in prior studies. To evaluate potential age and sex effects on model design, we also constructed the normative models by including sex and age into original predictor set. The results showed that there are significant spatial correlations between four different conditions (all p_spin < .001, Figure S5), implying that sex and age had no significant effect on our normative model. To evaluate the influences of medication effect, the Pearson correlation analysis was conducted between dose of medicine and individualized regional deviations in the patients with MDD, BD and SZ. There are no significant correlation between dose of medicine and individual regional deviations.

nm9_nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study performed internal validation using 10-fold cross-validation on the HCtrain group. This is same domain (healthy controls from Center for MRI Research, Peking University) but non-independent data (same dataset used for training). Performance metrics (SMSE and MSLL) were evaluated.
nm9_nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: The internal evaluation of model generalizability of normative functioning underlying emotional episodic memory was assessed using 10-fold cross-validation applied to HCtrain, and replicated estimation in HCtest. We assessed performance for the normative models for each brain region by evaluating the standardized mean-squared error (SMSE) and the mean standardized log-loss (MSLL) in HCtrain and HCtest cohort, respectively. A high internal generalizability of normative modelling was exhibited, showing with a SMSE close to 1 (HCtrain: 1.050 ± 0.030; HCtest: 1.047 ± 0.031) and a MSLL close to 0 (HCtrain: 0.029 ± 0.016; HCtest: 0.023 ± 0.026).

nm10_nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study performed external validation using an independent HCtest group (164 healthy controls from the clinical dataset) which represents same domain (healthy controls) but independent data (different participants from a different site - Center for Neuroimaging, Peking University Sixth Hospital). The validation assessed distribution similarity using Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and spatial correlation. Results showed no significant difference in distribution (K-S test = 0.087, p = .320) and high spatial correlation (r = 0.956, p_spin < .001) between HCtrain and HCtest regional deviation maps.
nm10_nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: The testing sample that comprised the clinical dataset (HCtest group) was positioned on the normative percentile charts for replicate validation and individualized evaluation. As external validation, we positioned each participant in HCtest within the normative range and further calculated the subject-level distribution similarity between HCtrain and HCtest cohort using Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and the spatial-level distribution similarity using spatial correction analysis with spatial autocorrelation corrected. There was no significant difference of the distribution of mean regional normative z scores between HCtrain and HCtest (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, K-S = 0.087, p = .320). Mean regional deviation map in HCtrain and HCtest was highly associated (r = 0.956, p_spin < .001, 10,000 times permutation tests with spatial autocorrelation).
nm10_nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.location: Main text, Normative Model section; Supplementary Page 11-12

caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Z-score derived from normative model; extreme deviations defined as |z| > 2.6 (p < .005); percentage of individuals showing extreme deviations; Δ percentage map (difference between percentage maps of clinical group and HCtest)
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The study clearly describes multiple deviation metrics: (1) Individual z-scores quantifying deviation from normative reference for each brain region; (2) Extreme deviations thresholded at |z| > 2.6 (corresponding to p < .005); (3) Percentage maps showing proportion of individuals with extreme deviations; (4) Δ percentage maps representing group differences. Additional validation using threshold-weighted analysis was also performed.
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: We derived a z value from a model that quantified the deviation from the normative reference for each participant in any given brain region, which can be defined as a measurement of individualized alterations. To investigate brain regions with significant extreme deviations, we further defined extreme deviations by thresholding the individualized deviation (z value) derived from normative modeling using z of ±2.6 (corresponding to p < .005 in a standard normal distribution). A percentage map quantifying the proportion of individuals showing an extreme deviation was calculated for each group, separately for positive and negative extreme deviations. The proportion difference (Δ percentage map) of individuals with extreme deviations was assessed between each diagnostic group with the HCtest group.
caa6_deviation_metric.location: Main text, Statistical Analysis of Individual Extreme Deviations section; Supplementary Page 5

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Multiple linear regression with leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) to predict clinical affective symptoms from individual regional deviations; Pearson correlation and RMSE between observed and predicted scores; non-parametric permutation test (10,000 permutations) for statistical significance (p_perm < .05); virtual lesion analysis to determine feature weights of regions and networks. Affective symptoms measures: MDD - anxiety/somatization factor from HAMD; BD - total HAMD scores; SZ - anxiety/depression factor from PANSS. Group-based permutation tests (10,000 permutations) with FDR correction were used to identify significant regional and network-level differences.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Distinct patterns of macroscale neural dysfunctions during emotional memory were embedded in non-overlapping emotional networks specific to each disorder (MDD: EN3-emotion perception/generation; BD: EN2/EN4-cognitive appraisal and emotional reactivity; SZ: EN1-working memory/response inhibition) and significantly associated with affective symptoms, with disorder-specific cellular signatures (oligodendrocytes converged across disorders; microglia for MDD, astrocytes for BD, excitatory neurons for SZ).
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Using normative modeling of fMRI activation during emotional episodic memory, the study revealed heterogeneous individual deviations with approximately 50% of patients showing extreme deviations in at least one brain region. Macroscale alterations showed little spatial overlap across disorders but were embedded in distinct large-scale emotional networks: MDD patients exhibited supranormal deviations in EN3 (emotion perception and generation, Δ percentage = 8.84%, p = .013 FDR-corrected), BD patients showed infranormal deviations in EN2 (cognitive appraisal, Δ percentage = 16.66%, p = .009) and EN4 (emotional reactivity, Δ percentage = 19.71%, p = .001), and SZ patients demonstrated infranormal deviations in EN1 (working memory and response inhibition, Δ percentage = 8.21%, p = .025). These network-specific deviations significantly predicted affective symptoms: anxiety/somatization factor in MDD (r = 0.295, p_perm = .032, RMSE = 2.324), total HAMD scores in BD (r = 0.415, p_perm = .020, RMSE = 18.515), and anxiety/depression factor in SZ (r = 0.319, p_perm = .007, RMSE = 5.297). Shared regional hyperactivation was observed in right amygdala, left insula, and right supramarginal gyrus across all disorders. At the microscale level, imaging transcriptomic analysis revealed transdiagnostic convergence in oligodendrocytes, with disorder-specific cellular signatures: microglia enrichment for MDD (both infra- and supranormal deviations), astrocytes for BD (infranormal deviations), and excitatory neurons for SZ (both directions). Individual-level cell-type enrichment scores for these specific cell types showed replicable significant correlations with affective symptoms across two independent single-cell datasets.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study demonstrates the utility of normative modeling for disentangling individual heterogeneity in task-based fMRI data and mapping cross-scale alterations (from genes/cells to networks to symptoms) in psychiatric disorders. The disorder-specific emotional network disruptions and their predictive weights for affective symptoms offer potential targets for optimizing clinical treatment strategies. Circuit-level analysis using lesion network mapping revealed that dysfunctional circuits aligned with disorder-specific emotional networks, suggesting that circuit-level interactions drive affective symptoms. Virtual lesion analysis confirmed that disorder-specific emotional networks (EN3 for MDD, EN4 for BD, EN1 for SZ) exhibited maximum predictive weight for affective symptoms. The findings suggest that cellular abnormalities may act as vulnerability factors shaping macroscale dysfunctions and clinical outcomes.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: 1) Relatively small clinical sample sizes (MDD n=56, BD n=31, SZ n=73), especially for transdiagnostic analysis, limiting ability to parse clinical heterogeneity; 2) Non-overlapping affective symptom measures across disorders (different subscales/total scores used); 3) Most BD patients were in euthymic stage, limiting generalizability across mood states; 4) Medication effects: despite sensitivity analysis showing no significant correlation with deviations, possibility of confounding cannot be entirely ruled out (MDD: 66% on medication, SZ: 53%, BD: variable medications); 5) Gene expression data from AHBA based on only 6 healthy donors may not fully represent cortical gene expression variability; 6) Gene expression limited to left hemisphere; 7) Cell-type enrichment based on indirect spatial correlation between independent imaging and transcriptomic datasets rather than within-subject measurements; 8) Potential site differences between HCtrain and clinical datasets not explicitly addressed through harmonization.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This study represents a comprehensive multi-scale investigation combining normative modeling of task-fMRI with imaging transcriptomics and cell-type enrichment analysis. Key methodological strengths include: 1) Use of emotional episodic memory task with established relevance to affective symptoms; 2) Robust validation including 10-fold cross-validation, external validation with independent HC sample, different brain atlases (DK, AAL, Brainnetome), and threshold-weighted deviation analysis; 3) Multi-level analysis spanning regional, network, and circuit levels; 4) Integration of two independent cell-type gene marker datasets (Lake et al. and Li et al.) for replication of cellular findings. The study addresses an important gap by linking individual-level deviations to dimensional affective symptoms across diagnostic categories. Age range was restricted (18-43 years) and participants were Chinese Han ancestry, which may limit generalizability. The same scanner model (3T GE Discovery MR750) was used at both sites. Inclusion criteria: Chinese Han ancestry, age 18-43, right-handed. Exclusion criteria for HC: neurological/psychiatric disease, loss of consciousness >5min, pregnancy/lactation, MRI contraindications. Additional exclusion for patients: other DSM-IV axis I/II diagnoses, substance abuse, severe physical diseases, narrow-angle glaucoma, epilepsy history, ECT within 6 months. Ethics approval from Peking University Sixth Hospital (Ethics Review No. 32 of 2013 for Healthy dataset; No. 32 of 2015 for BD, No. 32 of 2017 for MDD, No. 2 of 2021 for SZ and HCtest). Statistical threshold for regional differences: p < .0167 (.05/3) with FDR correction accounting for 3 group comparisons. Network-level significance: p < .05 FDR-corrected. The emotional episodic memory task elicited robust memory-enhancing effects for emotional stimuli across all groups (all p < .001), validating the task manipulation.
